article.headline: The Price Level That Hurts the Most Options Buyers
article.lede: Every options expiration, a peculiar gravitational force is said to pull stock prices toward a single strike: the point of *maximum pain*, where the greatest aggregate loss falls on options buyers. Whether that pull is real, imagined, or self-fulfilling is a question academics have argued for two decades.
article.body:
Options markets carry a dirty secret that every expiration week refreshes: the house, in the form of *market makers* (the dealers who take the other side of retail and institutional options trades), profits most when options expire worthless. *Maximum pain theory* formalises this intuition into a specific number. For any given expiration, you sum the dollar losses that all outstanding calls and puts would sustain at each possible closing price, and the strike where that aggregate loss is largest — for buyers, not sellers — is the max pain level. The theory then makes a bold claim: prices tend to drift there.

The mechanism proposed is not conspiracy but mechanics. Market makers, having sold options in bulk, must continuously *delta hedge* — buying and selling shares to keep their exposure roughly neutral as prices move. When a stock sits above the max pain strike, dealers who are short calls face rising delta and must sell stock, nudging prices down. When a stock sits below, dealers short puts must buy stock, nudging prices up. The hedging activity, the theory argues, acts like a rubber band, snapping prices toward the level of maximum option-holder pain as expiration nears.

The empirical record is genuinely mixed, though not entirely dismissive. A landmark 2005 study by Ni, Pearson, and Poteshman in the *Journal of Financial Economics* documented statistically significant *price pinning* — stocks closing suspiciously close to option strike prices on expiration Fridays — with closing-price distortions averaging roughly 16.5 basis points and aggregate market-cap effects exceeding nine billion dollars per expiration cycle. A 2022 portfolio study found that buying high-max-pain stocks and shorting low-max-pain stocks generated positive abnormal returns, particularly in the week of expiration, and particularly for institutional (not retail) participants. Yet practitioner consensus is more deflating: one widely cited rule of thumb holds that max pain "works" only thirty to forty percent of the time — better than coin-flipping, but nowhere near a trading edge worth betting heavily on.

The effect is also sharply time-dependent. Its predictive power increases inside the three-day window before expiration (the *0DTE to 2DTE* zone, meaning zero-to-two days to expiry) and dissolves almost entirely more than a week out. Any earnings release, macro surprise, or broad liquidity event can overwhelm the gravitational pull completely. High-open-interest underlyings like *SPX* and *SPY* — the S&P 500 index and its ETF proxy, each carrying enormous options volume — show the most consistent pinning behaviour; thinly traded single names show little to none.

The account @maximumpain333, whose display name is Maxpein, takes its handle from the theory but its posting diet runs elsewhere entirely. Visible posts from the account in 2025 cover human biofields, piezoelectric body mechanics, wireless-body-area-network surveillance concerns, planetary alignment, and metaphysical takes on scripture — a content mix that sits in the spiritual-conspiratorial corner of the platform rather than the options-trading one. The handle is an allusion, not a profession. The specific tweet bookmarked here, posted around April 22, 2025 and drawing 403,000 impressions, could not be recovered: X's paywall returned a 402 error to unauthenticated fetches, and no cached or archived version was located. Its engagement numbers — 2,500 reposts and 18,000 likes against that impression count — suggest viral reach typical of spiritually or emotionally resonant content rather than dry financial analysis.

Max pain theory, whatever its predictive limits, endures because it gives traders a framework for an otherwise opaque question: where do the big players need prices to land? The answer is never certain, but the question itself is the right one. In a market increasingly dominated by short-dated options flow, understanding where dealer hedging creates gravitational pockets is less mysticism than structural literacy — even if the theory's namesake account has, apparently, moved on to higher frequencies.

concepts.definition: The hypothesis that stock prices tend to drift toward the options strike price at which aggregate losses for options buyers — and thus aggregate payouts from option sellers — would be largest at expiration. Derived from market-maker delta-hedging mechanics.

The practice by which options market makers continuously buy or sell shares of the underlying stock to offset changes in their options' directional exposure (delta), keeping their net position roughly market-neutral.

The documented tendency for optionable stocks to close at or very near an option strike price on expiration day, more frequently than random chance would predict, likely due to concentrated hedging activity around those strikes.

The total number of outstanding options contracts that have not yet been settled or closed. High open interest at a particular strike concentrates dealer hedging activity and amplifies max pain effects.
Options contracts expiring the same trading day they are traded. The 0–2 DTE window is where max pain's gravitational pull, if real, is most acute.
